analysis.title: Hotter US inflation strengthens the case for a December Fed hike
key_insights: October US CPI rose 0.4% month-on-month on headline and 0.3% on core, both 0.1ppt above consensus.
No year-on-year CPI rates were published because the government shutdown meant no price data was collected in October 2025.

Details were mixed. New vehicle prices rose 0.2% m/m and used vehicle prices fell 1.2%, while medical care commodities rose 0.5%, transportation services rose 0.8% and shelter, the largest CPI component, rose 0.3%.

Fed Governor Chris Waller said earlier on 10 November that he backs a 25bp hike in December and could opt for 50bp. After Waller's comments and the CPI print, the 10Y Treasury yield rose 6bp and the 2Y rose 13bp.
Markets now fully price a 25bp December hike, in line with ING's forecast, versus 20bp priced before Waller's comments.

Hopes of Middle East de-escalation are lowering energy costs, with retail gasoline below $4/gallon for the first time since mid-July. ING expects this to be a meaningful drag on November headline inflation.
November CPI data will not be released until the day after the December FOMC meeting, though the Fed may get a preview of it, which could give it confidence to hike only 25bp.
ING does not forecast any further hikes in 2027, as interest rate-sensitive sectors cool, and housing costs, lower energy prices and weak wage growth dampen price pressures.

tension_points.bull_case: Hotter CPI and Waller's backing of a hike, including a possible 50bp move, argue for a larger hike. Markets fully price 25bp.
tension_points.bear_case: Falling gasoline prices should drag on November headline inflation, and the Fed may get a preview of that data, which could give it confidence to hike only 25bp.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A preview of November CPI data showing a meaningful energy-driven drop in headline inflation before the December FOMC meeting would support a 25bp hike over 50bp.
